papers.title: Vigilance, Risk Vulnerability, and the Precautionary Augment
papers.abstract: Risk raises the expected marginal utility of a prudent agent. We define this proportional change as the precautionary augment, which measures risk-induced changes in the marginal value of saving, the Lucas Tree risk-free rate, and asset prices in a derivative-saturated market where market-state securities provide incomplete coverage against idiosyncratic risk. One agent is more vigilant than another if their precautionary augment is larger for all unfair risks. We derive and compare conditions for greater vigilance, showing how to implement the Diffidence Theorem geometrically. Because risk vulnerability is equivalent to decreasing vigilance, classic results about risk vulnerability emerge as corollaries.

papers.title: The Main Monetary Policy Shock
papers.abstract: We propose a novel procedure to identify a main monetary policy (MMP) shock as the linear combination of monetary policy surprises that best explains macroeconomic fluctuations. Implemented with two standard high-frequency yield-curve surprises and the Boehm and Kroner (2024) non-yield shock, the MMP shock explains nontrivial business-cycle variation over the last 30 years, in contrast with prior findings. Moreover, the MMP shock differs markedly from a textbook monetary policy shock: a contractionary shock leaves interest rates mostly unchanged but persistently lowers headline prices and appreciates the dollar, while temporarily tightening financial conditions and depressing industrial production.

papers.title: Unconventional Monetary Policy and Deposit Retention
papers.abstract: The two dimensions of unconventional monetary policy — holding the short rate at the zero-lower bound (ZLB) and quantitative easing (QE) — shifted deposit composition toward more interest-sensitive customers. The ZLB drew these customers by creating rate compression, which limited the benefit of searching for high-yielding liquidity sources. QE also drew rate-sensitive, large depositors from the Federal Reserve’s purchases of bonds from non-banks. Once policy normalized, flow sensitivity and the deposit beta both increased with exposure to QE and the ZLB. We conclude that unconventional monetary policy made deposit retention costlier and riskier for banks.
